title: The source reads version 1 in its metadata table and v2 in its file name
source: Recovery Workbench Audit and Logging Design v2.docx
description: The metadata table of the source document reads 'Version | 1' and 'Date | 28 October 2026', while the file name is 'Recovery Workbench Audit and Logging Design v2.docx'. Two readings are possible: the metadata row was not raised when the file was reissued as version 2, or the file name is the family version and the table is the document's own issue number. The reading decides what the next version is called and which number the change log carries.
evidence: Source metadata table rows 'Version | 1' and 'Date | 28 October 2026'; file name 'Recovery Workbench Audit and Logging Design v2.docx'; core properties title 'Recovery Workbench Audit and Logging Design v2' and revision 1.
owner_role: Document owner of the audit and logging design
proposed: Take the file name as the family version, so this document becomes version 3, and keep the source values in a 'Source version' row: 1, 28 October 2026. The change log carries both readings.

title: The local decision record has no table, no DDL and no case or trace column
source: Recovery Workbench Audit and Logging Design v2.docx; Recovery Workbench Architecture v5; Recovery Workbench Temporal and Drools Design v1
description: Architecture v5 makes every service write a decision record in its own schema in the same transaction as the state change, and the Temporal and Drools design gives the field list (chain_seq, inputsRef, ruleId, ruleVersion, recommendation, approverUserId, approvalLevel, finalCall, actions, outcome, decidedAt, prev_hash, entry_hash). No source names the table, gives its DDL, or says which column holds the case reference and the trace ID, which the source document requires for tracing. The ten fields of the source also do not map one to one: entry_id and case_id have no column of their own in the target list.
evidence: Architecture v5 slide 20 ('Writes its own decision records locally and publishes DecisionRecorded') and slide 28 ('each service writes a decision record in its own schema in the same transaction as the state change'); Temporal and Drools Design v1 decision record field list; source section 2 field table and section 3 trace bullets; the Ownership Map v1 lists table decision_log_entry for P7 only and no local record table.
owner_role: Service owners of the 19 services with P7 rwb-decision
proposed: Each service creates its local decision-record table in its own schema through the decision-record library, with the target field list and a reference to the case and the trace ID in inputsRef; the name and DDL are settled in the DB story of each service.

title: The access log has an API and an owner but no table in the Ownership Map
source: Recovery Workbench Microservice Ownership Map v1
section: 1 The records and 7 Owners and contracts
description: The source puts the access log inside the decision log store. Version 3 places it in rwb_access (P4) with the API GET /admin/access-log, which the Ownership Map assigns to P4. The map holds no access_log table, so the store of the access log, its append-only mechanism and its chain are undocumented, although the source requires inserts only and a hash chain.
evidence: Source section 1 (access log 'inside the decision log store') and section 4 (inserts only); Ownership Map v1 Read me and Tables sheets have no access_log row; ownership.json api has 'GET /admin/access-log' with owner P4 and no table entry.
proposed: The access log is an append-only table in rwb_access (P4) behind GET /admin/access-log; the DB story of P4 creates it and the contract story publishes the read path.

title: Where the retention period of the ledgers and the access log is held, and which job enforces it
source: Recovery Workbench Audit and Logging Design v2.docx; Recovery Workbench Microservice Ownership Map v1
description: The source sets the decision log, the interaction ledger and the access log retention by Compliance (DL26) and gives a period only for application logs. In the target the retention tables retention_rule and retention_action belong to rwb-document (P5) and JOB-17 runs retention in rwb-document, which is document retention. No source states where the ledger and access-log retention periods are stored, which service enforces them, or whether the daily seal and the WORM copy follow the same period.
evidence: Source section 5 table (DL26 for the three ledgers); ownership.json tables retention_rule and retention_action with owner P5 and jobs JOB-17 (P5, retention); Architecture v5 slide 44 job map; no retention row for the decision ledger or the access log.
owner_role: Service owners P7 rwb-decision, P1 rwb-source-data and P4 rwb-access with Compliance
proposed: Keep every period as written and mark the owner open: P7 enforces the ledger period, P1 the interaction ledger and P4 the access log, each as a row of its own retention data, until Compliance states where the periods are held.

title: The nightly copy to the data lake survives in the source and in the v4 batch design
source: Recovery Workbench Audit and Logging Design v2.docx; Recovery Workbench Architecture v5
description: The source sends a nightly copy of the decision log to the data lake and makes the daily chain check a job. Architecture v5 removes the data lake (INT-19 and INT-20 removed) and replaces the copy with continuous Kafka ingest (JOB-13) and a daily ledger seal to write-once storage (JOB-14 checks the chain). The batch design of the previous version still copies the log to the lake at 01:00.
evidence: Source section 1 (decision log 'ACE database; nightly copy to the data lake'); Architecture v5 slide 37 ('No data lake'), slide 14 (daily ledger seal, WORM) and slide 44 (JOB-13, JOB-14); Batch and Scheduling Design v4 JOB-13 (nightly copy to the data lake, 01:00).
proposed: Remove the data lake copy and its job; keep JOB-13 as the continuous ingest, JOB-14 as the chain check and the daily seal to write-once storage as the archival control. RWB-E1-014 stays retired and its dependencies are dropped.

title: The interaction ledger is claimed by rwb-case and by rwb-source-data
source: Recovery Workbench Audit and Logging Design v2.docx; Technical Specifications by Module v5
section: 1 The records and 7 Owners and contracts
description: The source gives the interaction ledger no owner beyond 'ACE database'. The plan default ruling puts the ledger in rwb-source-data (P1) and DP-18 confirms it, while the latest module specifications define the interaction table and the two interaction endpoints in rwb-case (P3), and the API specification marks them x-module P3. The ownership ruling exists in the plan, but the source modules still disagree.
evidence: Source section 1 (interaction ledger, 'ACE database'); Template and Rules v1 R3 default ruling (interaction ledger to P1) and R5.5 DP-18; TSD P3 v3 T3.1 (interaction); API Specification v4 x-module P3 for GET and POST /cases/{caseId}/interactions; ownership.json rulings for interaction and efs_ledger_outcome (P1).
owner_role: Service owner P1 rwb-source-data with P3 rwb-case
proposed: The ledger and its writer stay with P1 and rwb-case reads it through the P1 contract, as the plan ruling says; the module specifications are corrected in the same wave.

title: The approver identifier is personal data under a rule that forbids personal data in records
source: Recovery Workbench Audit and Logging Design v2.docx; Recovery Workbench Temporal and Drools Design v1
section: 2 The decision log entry and 6 What is never logged
description: The source records 'who decided' in the decision log and forbids personal fields in logs, traces and prompts. The target field is approverUserId, an identifier that is personal data under PDPA. No source states whether the identifier is stored in clear, tokenised, or held only as a protected reference, or how an auditor reads it back under the masking rules of rwb-access.
evidence: Source section 2 row 'decided_by, approval_level, limit_applied' and section 6 ('Personal fields in application logs, traces or agent prompts'); Temporal and Drools Design v1 decision record list (approverUserId); Architecture v5 slide 30 (audit and PII access logs to SOC).
owner_role: Service owner P7 rwb-decision with P4 rwb-access and Compliance
proposed: Store the identifier, never a name; mask it in every export under the masking rows of rwb-access (P4) and record the read in the PII log. The protection of the column itself is a decision for Compliance and Information Security.

title: One chain or 19 chains plus the ledger chain
description: The source has one hash-chained decision log checked by one daily job. The target has a hash chain in every service and a second chain in the central ledger, anchored daily to write-once storage. No source states the scope of each chain (per service, per case or global), what prev_hash holds for the first record of a service, or which chain an auditor treats as the chain of record when the two disagree.
evidence: Source section 4 (one chain, one daily job); Architecture v5 slide 28 ('hash-linked to the previous record', 'chain verification', 'daily anchor of the ledger hash to immutable (WORM) storage'); Temporal and Drools Design v1 (chain_seq, prev_hash, entry_hash per record).
owner_role: Service owner P7 rwb-decision with the 19 service owners
proposed: Each service chains its own records in chain_seq order, the ledger chains its entries on ingest, and the daily WORM fingerprint covers the ledger chain; the chain of record is the ledger, with the local chain available for a replay.

title: The record that governs while the central ledger lags by up to five minutes
section: 3 Tracing an action end to end and 4 Integrity
description: Version 3 keeps the local record authoritative in the transaction and gives the ledger a five-minute completeness target with gap alerts. The source requires the decision log to be searchable, but no source states what the audit search returns for a decision that is committed and not yet in the ledger, whether the ledger marks the entry as pending, or whether a strict-mode step must wait for a pending entry of another service.
evidence: Architecture v5 slide 28 ('rwb-decision reads rwb.decision-record.v1 into the ledger within 5 minutes', 'gap alerts', strict mode for irreversible steps); source section 3 (search by case, rule, approver or date) and section 4 (a failed write raises an incident).
proposed: The audit search reads the ledger only and shows an entry as not yet sealed until JOB-13 has collected it; the local record is reached through the owning service's contract and strict mode waits for the ledger acknowledgement of its own record.

title: The versions in force in the access log come from two services
source: Recovery Workbench Audit and Logging Design v2.docx; Recovery Workbench Architecture v5
section: 1 The records and 7 Owners and contracts
description: The access log holds 'versions in force'. The rule and model versions are governed in rwb-decision (P7) and loaded by each owning service, while the access log is written in rwb-access (P4). No source states whether the access row carries the version the service actually applied, the version the registry published, or both, and which service writes it.
evidence: Source section 1 access log row ('versions in force'); Architecture v5 slide 14 (P7 rule registry) and slide 41 (P4 roles, scope, masking, DoA); Temporal and Drools Design v1 (owning service loads the version in force on RulePackageInForce, EV-30).
owner_role: Service owners P4 rwb-access and P7 rwb-decision
proposed: The access row records the version the owning service applied at the time of the event, and the registry in rwb-decision stays the source of the version and its effective date.
